performers: Soojin Han, violin; Hankyung Arte Philharmonic; Seokwon Hong, conductor
question: How does a short link turn minor into major without a break?
intro: A fourteen-bar passage in E minor for the soloist and strings follows the Andante directly and leads, through a long swell and a pause, to a fanfare and a finale whose home key is E major. Follow the soloist’s fast opening theme, a brief second theme in B major, and a coda that rushes to the end. All three movements of this set come from one live concert.

Recapitulation · main theme returns

cues.title: The Andante runs straight on
cues.text: The Andante is joined to the finale without a break: a fourteen-bar passage in E minor for the soloist and strings alone, marked Allegretto non troppo. Wikipedia says the linking was designed to eliminate applause between movements. This file begins on that link.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia describes the fourteen-bar E minor passage for solo violin and strings and the purpose of the linking; the score (printed p. 37) shows the Allegretto non troppo for the soloist and strings directly after the Andante’s last chord. The level is −20.3 dB at 0:00 and −17.2 dB at 0:15 with 0.0–1.0 detected onsets per second; the key estimates (E major, B minor) reflect the prominent E and B and are not read as chords.

cues.title: The first movement’s melody, again
cues.text: Wikipedia says the melody of this link is similar to the first movement’s opening, which hints that the concerto is cyclic. Listen for the soloist’s long, singing line over soft strings, with few notes per second, recalling where the concerto began.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s analysis says the link’s melody is similar to that of the opening; this is a listening suggestion, not a measured match. Detected onsets are 0.0–1.0 per second at 0:05–0:20 and the level is −19.0 dB at 0:05, −30.1 dB at 0:10 and −17.2 dB at 0:15.

cues.title: A swell on the dominant
cues.text: At about 0:24 the link’s melody gives way to a swell: the level rises from −27 dB to −15 dB in five seconds, and the bass stays on B, the dominant of E. In the score the winds and brass still rest here; only the soloist and strings sound.
cues.evidence: The report has a boundary at 0:24 (0.65); the level is −26.6 dB at 0:25 and −14.6 dB at 0:30; the bass is B at 0:25–0:35 and the key estimate is B major (0.85–0.87). The score (printed p. 37) shows the winds and brass resting, with fermatas, across the Allegretto non troppo.

cues.title: The pause before the dance
cues.text: After the swell the music falls almost silent: the level sinks to −31 dB at 0:40 and −44 dB at 0:45, the quietest window in the file. In the score the strings fade to pianissimo and a pause follows, the breath before the fanfare and the soloist’s fast theme.
cues.evidence: The level falls from −19.4 dB at 0:35 to −31.1 dB at 0:40 and −43.8 dB at 0:45, with 0.0 detected onsets at 0:40 and 0:45; the 0:40 and 0:45 windows are among the five quietest; the report has a boundary at 0:40 (0.50). The score (printed p. 37) shows the diminuendo to pianissimo and the fermatas before “Allegro molto vivace”.

cues.title: The fanfare and the fast theme
cues.text: At about 0:50 the Allegro molto vivace arrives with fortissimo chords, a fanfare that Wikipedia says is led by the trumpets, and the soloist’s fast opening theme follows at once. The level jumps by more than twenty decibels from the pause, and the home key of the finale is E major.
cues.evidence: The level rises from −43.8 dB at 0:45 to −19.3 dB at 0:50, and detected onsets from 0.0 to 2.2 per second at 0:50 and 5.4 per second at 1:05; the report has a boundary at 0:50 (0.60). Wikipedia describes the trumpet-led fanfare, the opening theme with fast passage-work and E major as the movement’s key; the score (printed p. 37) shows fortissimo chords in the bassoons, horns, trumpets and timpani at “Allegro molto vivace”, with the soloist’s entry in the same bar.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Perpetual motion
cues.text: From about 1:05 to 1:35 the detected note activity holds at five or six a second, with the level steady near −17 dB. The soloist’s quick figuration hardly stops, and from about 1:20 the key estimate settles on E major.
cues.evidence: Detected onsets are 5.4, 5.4, 6.0, 5.6, 5.4, 5.2 and 5.0 per second at 1:05–1:35; the level is between −13.6 and −18.9 dB; the key estimate is E major (0.74–0.86) at 1:20–1:45. Detected onsets are not note counts.

cues.title: A shadow of C♯ minor
cues.text: At about 1:50 the key estimate swings to C♯ minor, the relative minor of E, for a few seconds before the music moves on towards B major. Listen for the brief darkening that follows the bright E major.
cues.evidence: The key estimate is C♯ minor (0.63–0.71) at 1:50–1:55, between E major (0.74–0.86) at 1:20–1:45 and B major (0.73–0.91) at 2:00–2:35; the report has a boundary at 1:58 (0.45). The estimates are approximate.

cues.title: The second theme, in B major
cues.text: At about 2:00 the soloist plays a brief second theme in B major, the dominant. For half a minute the key estimate is B major and the bass stays on B. Wikipedia describes this as a brief B major theme for the soloist.
cues.evidence: The key estimate is B major (0.73–0.91) at 2:00–2:35 with the bass on B or F♯ and the level between −11.1 and −17.3 dB; the report has a boundary at 1:58 (0.45). Wikipedia says the second theme is a brief B major theme for the soloist.

cues.title: Arpeggios up and down
cues.text: Wikipedia says the second theme builds to rapidly rising and falling arpeggios, recalling the first movement’s cadenza. From about 2:20 the detected note activity climbs from about two a second to a peak near five at 2:30, then falls back by 2:40 as the level eases.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia describes the series of rapidly ascending and descending arpeggios after the second theme. Detected onsets are 2.4, 3.4, 4.8, 3.4 and 1.8 per second at 2:20–2:40; the time is approximate and not aligned to the score.

cues.title: An instant success
cues.text: The concerto was well received at its first performance in Leipzig in 1845, and by the end of the nineteenth century it was already counted among the greatest violin concertos. Mendelssohn first conducted it himself on 23 October 1845, again with David as soloist.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s article gives the warm reception, the later reputation and the date of Mendelssohn’s first performance as conductor, 23 October 1845, with David as soloist; the IMSLP work page gives the premiere of 13 March 1845.

cues.title: The orchestra varies the theme
cues.text: At about 2:50 the orchestra plays a variation of the opening melody, after which a short development begins in G major, according to Wikipedia. The level rises from −23.5 dB at 2:45 to −14.3 dB at 2:50, and G sits in the bass at 3:00–3:10.
cues.evidence: The level is −23.5 dB at 2:45 and −14.3 dB at 2:50; the report has boundaries at 2:50 (0.43), 2:56 (0.59) and 3:12 (0.37); the key estimate is G major (0.72) at 3:00 and the bass is G at 3:00–3:10. Wikipedia describes the orchestra’s variation and the G major development.

cues.title: The loudest crest of the development
cues.text: At about 3:10 the orchestra reaches a crest near −8 dB, one of the loudest windows in the file, with the key estimate on D major. The development is short, and it pushes forward here before the music turns back.
cues.evidence: The level is −12.8 dB at 3:05, −7.9 dB at 3:10 and −15.4 dB at 3:15, and the 3:10 window is among the five loudest; the key estimate is D major (0.84) at 3:10–3:20. The shortness of the development is from Wikipedia.

cues.title: The recapitulation begins
cues.text: At about 3:44 comes the strongest structural boundary in the file, and the main theme returns. Wikipedia says the recapitulation is much like the exposition, with the addition of a counter-melody in the strings. By 4:00 the level dips to −29 dB while detected notes stay quick.
cues.evidence: The report’s strongest boundary is at 3:44 (novelty 1.00), with another at 3:34 (0.76); the key estimate is B major (0.79–0.81) at 3:40–3:45 and F♯ major (0.83) at 3:50; the level is −29.1 dB at 4:00 with 5.6 detected onsets per second, among the five quietest windows. Wikipedia describes the recapitulation and the string counter-melody.

cues.title: A model for later concertos
cues.text: Wikipedia says the placing of the first movement’s cadenza before the recapitulation was echoed in Tchaikovsky’s violin concerto, and that Sibelius used his cadenza to extend the development. After this concerto it became rare to leave a cadenza to be improvised. Liszt’s Second Piano Concerto also links its movements.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s “Legacy” section gives the Tchaikovsky and Sibelius cadenzas, the decline of improvised cadenzas and the influence of the linked movements on Liszt’s Second Piano Concerto; these are the article’s claims of influence, not documented borrowings.

cues.title: The second theme in E major
cues.text: At about 4:30 the second theme returns, now in the home key: the key estimate is E major at 0.86–0.92 from 4:30 to 4:45. In the exposition it was in B major, so the tonic now has the last word.
cues.evidence: The key estimate is B major at 4:25 (0.73), then E major (0.86, 0.92, 0.92, 0.87) at 4:30–4:45; the level is between −9.0 and −17.1 dB. Wikipedia says the second theme is repeated in the home key of E major.

cues.title: Six years of waiting
cues.text: Mendelssohn told David in July 1838 that he wanted to write him a violin concerto, then sketched it in at least two stages while David pleaded with him to finish. He worked on it seriously only in July 1844, once he had decided to shake off a wearying court appointment in Berlin.
cues.evidence: Steven Ledbetter’s Boston Symphony Orchestra note (https://www.bso.org/works/mendelssohn-violin-concerto) gives the July 1838 letter, the sketching in at least two stages, David’s urgent pleas, Mendelssohn’s decision to shake off the Berlin court appointment under Frederick William IV and the date July 1844; it does not date his release from the post.

cues.title: Trills over the tune
cues.text: Wikipedia says near the end of the movement the woodwinds play the main tune against prolonged trills from the soloist, a kind of small cadenza. In the score this is near the end of the last fifth of the movement, and the detected note activity falls to about one a second at 5:20.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia describes the woodwind tune against sustained trills; the score (printed p. 52) shows the trills in the solo part. The time is proportioned from page lengths and the report: detected onsets are 4.6 at 5:15 and 1.0 at 5:20, with the level at −9.1 dB and −10.7 dB, and the key estimate E major (0.73–0.81).
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The coda gathers
cues.text: At about 5:40 the coda begins. The bass sits on B, the dominant, while the level climbs to −7.6 dB at 5:50, one of the loudest windows in the file; by 6:05 the key estimate is E major for the final rush. Wikipedia calls this a frenetic coda.
cues.evidence: The report has a boundary at 5:40 (0.36); the bass is B at 5:40–6:30; the key estimate is B major (0.70–0.84) at 5:40–6:00 and E major (0.77–0.89) at 6:05–6:35; the level is −10.7 dB at 5:45 and −7.6 dB at 5:50, and the 5:50 window is among the five loudest. Wikipedia describes the frenetic coda.

cues.title: The final rush
cues.text: From about 6:05 to 6:35 the whole orchestra and the soloist stay near −9 dB in E major, with the loudest windows of the file at 6:10, 6:30 and 6:35. Listen for the soloist’s running notes riding above the orchestra to the end.
cues.evidence: The level is −12.4 dB at 6:05, −8.5 dB at 6:10, −9.0 dB at 6:15, −10.2 dB at 6:20, −9.5 dB at 6:25, −8.5 dB at 6:30 and −6.8 dB at 6:35; the 6:10, 6:30 and 6:35 windows are among the five loudest; the key estimate is E major (0.77–0.89) at 6:05–6:35.

cues.title: The last chords
cues.text: In the closing seconds, up to about 6:38, the concerto ends on E major chords: the detected note activity falls to 0.4 a second at 6:35 and the level reaches −6.8 dB, the loudest window of the file. Listen for how the soloist’s running notes give way to the orchestra’s final chords.
cues.evidence: At 6:35 the level is −6.8 dB with 0.4 detected onsets per second and the key estimate is E major (0.87); the file ends at 6:39.0 (399.0 s). The 6:35 window is the loudest of the file.

transitions.title: The link swells onto the dominant
transitions.from: Link · Allegretto non troppo, E minor
transitions.how: The Andante’s end gives way, without a break, to a fourteen-bar passage in E minor for the soloist and strings alone. At about 0:24 the link’s melody ends in a swell: the level rises from −27 dB to −15 dB in five seconds, with the bass on B, the dominant of E, and the key estimate on B major. The winds and brass rest throughout the link in the score. The minor-key passage ends by preparing the major key, so the finale’s E major, when it comes, arrives as a release.
transitions.evidence: The report has a boundary at 0:24 (0.65); the level is −26.6 dB at 0:25 and −14.6 dB at 0:30; the bass is B at 0:25–0:35 and the key estimate is B major (0.85–0.87). The link is from Wikipedia; the score (printed p. 37) shows the winds and brass resting across the Allegretto non troppo.

transitions.title: Silence, then fanfare and dance
transitions.to: Allegro molto vivace · fanfare and main theme
transitions.how: After the swell the sound falls to near silence: −31 dB at 0:40 and −44 dB at 0:45, with no detected attacks, as the strings fade to pianissimo and pause. At about 0:50 the Allegro molto vivace arrives with fortissimo chords in the brass, bassoons and timpani, a fanfare that Wikipedia says is led by the trumpets, and the soloist’s fast theme follows at once; the tempo changes sharply and the level rises more than twenty decibels. The key estimate stays on B major to 1:05 and settles on E major from 1:20.
transitions.evidence: The level is −19.4 dB at 0:35, −31.1 dB at 0:40, −43.8 dB at 0:45 and −19.3 dB at 0:50, with 0.0 detected onsets at 0:40–0:45 and 2.2–5.4 per second at 0:50–1:05; the report has boundaries at 0:40 (0.50) and 0:50 (0.60); the key estimate is B major (0.78–0.83) at 0:50–1:05. The score (printed p. 37) shows the diminuendo, the fermatas and the fortissimo chords at “Allegro molto vivace”.

transitions.title: From E major to the dominant
transitions.from: Allegro molto vivace · fanfare and main theme
transitions.how: The main theme runs in E major to about 1:45; at about 1:50 the key estimate dips briefly to C♯ minor, the relative minor, before B major, the dominant, arrives at about 2:00. The second theme is brief and played by the soloist, according to Wikipedia. As in the first movement’s exposition, the second theme sits on a related key: there G major, the relative major of E minor, here B major, the dominant of E major.
transitions.evidence: The key estimate is E major (0.74–0.86) at 1:20–1:45, C♯ minor (0.63–0.71) at 1:50–1:55 and B major (0.73–0.91) at 2:00–2:35; the report has a boundary at 1:58 (0.45). Wikipedia places the second theme in B major, played by the soloist.

transitions.title: The orchestra varies the theme; G major
transitions.how: After the arpeggios the level dips to −23.5 dB at 2:45, and at about 2:50 the orchestra plays a variation of the opening melody, as Wikipedia describes. The development that follows is short and moves to G major, a key a major third from B: G is in the bass at 3:00–3:10, and the level reaches a crest near −8 dB at 3:10. The orchestra, not the soloist, leads this join.
transitions.evidence: The level is −23.5 dB at 2:45, −14.3 dB at 2:50 and −7.9 dB at 3:10; the report has boundaries at 2:50 (0.43), 2:56 (0.59) and 3:12 (0.37); the key estimate is G major (0.72) at 3:00 and D major (0.84) at 3:10–3:20. Wikipedia describes the orchestral variation and the G major development.

transitions.title: A dip, then the main theme returns
transitions.how: The development’s keys settle back towards B major and F♯ major, the dominant side, by about 3:40–3:50, and the report’s strongest boundary, at 3:44, marks the return of the main theme. By 4:00 the level has dipped to −29 dB with the detected note activity still near five a second, a soft, quick passage; Wikipedia says the strings now add a counter-melody to the recapitulation of the exposition.
transitions.evidence: The report’s strongest boundary is at 3:44 (1.00); the key estimate is B major (0.79–0.81) at 3:40–3:45 and F♯ major (0.83) at 3:50; the level is −18.9 dB at 3:55 and −29.1 dB at 4:00, with 5.6 detected onsets per second. Wikipedia describes the recapitulation and the counter-melody.

transitions.title: The second theme comes home to E
transitions.how: The recapitulation moves, as the exposition did, towards the second theme. At about 4:30 the key estimate settles on E major at 0.86–0.92, so the theme that was in B major returns in the tonic. The sense of arrival is the opposite of the exposition’s: the second theme is no longer a visit to the dominant but a confirmation of the home key, and the level is steadier, between −9 and −15 dB.
transitions.evidence: The key estimate is F♯ minor (0.76) at 4:20, B major (0.73) at 4:25 and E major (0.86–0.92) at 4:30–4:45; the level is between −9.0 and −14.6 dB at 4:30–4:45. Wikipedia says the second theme is repeated in the home key of E major.

transitions.title: The dominant, then the final rush
transitions.how: After the woodwind tune over the soloist’s trills, the bass sits on B at about 5:40, the dominant of E, while the level climbs to −7.6 dB at 5:50. At about 6:05 the key estimate becomes E major for the coda, which Wikipedia calls frenetic. The music stands on the dominant, then releases into the tonic for the final rush to the last chords at 6:38.
transitions.evidence: The report has a boundary at 5:40 (0.36); the bass is B at 5:40–6:30; the key estimate is B major (0.70–0.84) at 5:40–6:00 and E major (0.77–0.89) at 6:05–6:35; the level is −10.7 dB at 5:45 and −7.6 dB at 5:50. Wikipedia describes the frenetic coda.

composer.epithet: A composer-conductor who turned quicksilver string writing, Bachian counterpoint and remembered landscapes into tightly organised concert music.
facts: Piano with Ludwig Berger; composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter in Berlin
Music director, Düsseldorf, 1833–35; Gewandhaus conductor, Leipzig, from 1835; founder of Leipzig Conservatoire, 1843
Brother of Fanny Hensel; married Cécile Jeanrenaud in 1837; five children
Symphonies, concert overtures, concertos, oratorios, chamber music and Songs without Words
composer.background:
Felix Mendelssohn was born in Hamburg in 1809 and grew up in Berlin, where his father Abraham’s banking wealth supported an unusually extensive education. His grandfather was the Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn; Felix and his siblings were baptised as Christians in 1816, and the family used the additional surname Bartholdy. He studied piano with Ludwig Berger and composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter, alongside his elder sister Fanny. The family’s concerts extended their classroom education with repeated opportunities to hear their own music, revise it and discuss it with experienced performers.

Zelter’s teaching joined Bach’s counterpoint to classical forms. The boy wrote string symphonies, concertos and chamber works before the pieces usually treated as his starting point. At sixteen he composed the E♭ major Octet, Op. 20, for four violins, two violas and two cellos. Its eight independent parts create different densities inside one ensemble: the first violin’s long ascent, the other instruments’ pulsing accompaniments and the finale’s fugal entries continually reshape the texture. The scherzo’s soft, rapid articulation became a recurrent technical problem in his later orchestral writing.
